utterances.text: Thank you. Whose responsibility was it, then, if there was fire, outgoing fire, from civilian zones?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there is firing, I told Madam Prosecutor that it's targeting or firing the army rather than just shooting. If someone is firing from a civilian zone, then he is to blame, for sure, but it does not absolve the one who returns fire from any guilt. It's not that you can indiscriminately fire at civilians. You have to target the specific military target and see what the collateral civilian damage would be in such a case. So that would be the reference to a proportion when returning fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we should briefly go through this question of returning fire. I asked you how accurate were the reports of the observers, and now I would like us to see 65 ter 23902. General, in document D3452, that is your report dated the 6th of January, 1994, we can read that in the Ilidza area more than 120 shells of various calibres fell and so on and so forth. And now let us look at what the UNPROFOR reports about the 6th of January. So please look at page 1 where it says that the Bosnian side fired 20 and received 815, and the Serbian side fired 502 and incoming 7. Can you tell us, how does this figure of 502 which we fired can fit with the 815 incoming in the Bosnian territory? How does that tally?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a question of proportionality. As far as I have understood your question. Now, in -- to what extent the proportionality was marked on either side. But if I return a little bit to the first report of my command and there we'll see that on the 6th of January, if I'm right, that means Christmas Eve because the 7th of January is the Orthodox Christmas, they wished us a Merry Christmas in that way too. We can assess for ourselves whether, as I said, that was adequate or not. That was a term that we used. Now, this is a matter of assessment, where the shells fell, what were the targets, were so many shells needed. What was the military goal of such a use of artillery on both sides, and what were the decisions taken by the commanders? Did they decide just to neutralise a target or did they make the decision to destroy the targets? I said here that there is a distinction between the decisions and that that changes the number of shells that may be too great.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. I wanted to ask you this about accuracy: You reported that 120 shells landed on Ilidza only, whereas they reported that only 7 landed in the Serb territory. Can you tell us now, on the basis of the maths deduced from these two lines, can one draw a conclusion on the proportionality and adequacy of return fire? 300, 500, 600 shells. Can they say that the return fire from the Serb side was inadequate or inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have this report from the United Nations or UNPROFOR at the time to be able to gauge this. Now that I have this report before me, I had the report that was produced by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the differences are enormous, and I can't tell you what the source of this difference was, but the differences are so obvious that they don't call for a comment at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you not challenge that the SRK report mentioned 120 shells landed -- landing on Ilidza only?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do I challenge the accuracy of the figures in the SRK report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In a certain way I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we see the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I have no difficulty admitting this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. And just to clarify my position, the -- the map that the General discussed in his evidence in chief of the UNMO deployment and that we came back to did not show any UNMOs deployed in Ilidza. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit this one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you upload the SRK report that referred to 120 shells landing in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D3452. Both reports were sent out at 6.00 p.m., both the UNPROFOR report and the SRK report. They describe the situation as at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, somewhere in line 12 it says that over 120 shells landed in Ilidza of varied calibre, predominantly 82. Were you allowed to, and did you send strictly confidential and false reports to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, I would like to thank the Prosecutor for saying that they didn't have military observers over there and were not able to count how many shells landed in Ilidza. Thank you for that. Now, as for the second part of my answer to you, Mr. President, certainly we sent our reports on the basis of the reports that we received from subordinate commands and on the basis of reconnaissance, monitoring and all other intelligence and security measures which describe what the situation was like. The reports which speak specifically about the activities of the various forces and the various figures are accurate, and there should be no mistakes there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If this pleases the Chamber, we may call a different document. Perhaps we could ask the Trial Chamber to ask the Prosecution whether they still maintain that inaccurate reports were sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D1639, a day earlier. Let's see what the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had to report on to the Main Staff. I hope that all the participants will receive a translation. Can this be enlarged?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a day earlier, on the 5th of January, your deputy, Milosevic, states that the enemy was active in Grbavica, Dobrinja, Lukavica. A shell landed on the barracks even between the cafeteria and the kitchen. At 2030, a strong infantry attack from artillery mortars 82 and 122 millimetres. The attack was respelled without any consequences. General, sir, the previous report of the UN applied to the 5th and 6th of January until 1800 hours. Can you tell us if your deputy accurately reported and if the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps mounted attacks on the town or, in fact, defended itself?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this information in this period, the first half of January, that is, we can see that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was engaged in defensive action at the time. There was not even what you call active defence. The manoeuvre of forces can be, of course, demonstrated through forces and fire, and there may have been fire in this sense even.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be MFI'd, admitted and MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter 23905. This is probably an UNMO daily sitrep for Sector Sarajevo for the 4th and 5th of January, 1995. Since it's in English, I'll introduce it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when a thousand shells, say, is set to have landed on Sarajevo? Where would these shells normally land?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thousand shells, if they landed on Sarajevo, in that case Sarajevo would have looked differently at the time and still today, had this been the case. If there was fire and if there was an exchange of fire or return fire, counter fire as the artillery-speak would have it, it would have been fired at the enemy positions in the various areas according to the disposition, the layout that we are already aware of because we had them on the map. And if they opened fire, they would open fire from those same sectors, and the return fire would be targeting these sectors. Not the zones themselves because zones are wider, but to be more precise, it would be the enemy position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see item 2. Can we scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under item 2 it is stated that -- that there was outgoing 56 rounds on the Bosnian side and the Serbs sustained 30 hits. We don't know where those 26 shells fired by the Muslims landed, but it says here: "Approximately 80 per cent [In English] of incoming fire on both sides was on the confrontation line, 20 per cent in residential area." [Interpretation] Is this what you said a moment ago, that fire was opened not at neighbourhoods but that the fire was intended for the separation lines?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, we always say "separation lines," but of course fire can target the depth of the territory depending on where fire was opened from. We have to say that fire was targeting enemy targets on both sides, but of course, at least 20 per cent, according to what UNPROFOR says, went on civilian areas. Can this be tolerated or not? I don't know, but it has to probably fall into that portion of -- of proportionality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These -- the 20 per cent that did not hit the targets, was it the civilian population that was being targeted in that percentage or was there in the midst of it all something that could constitute a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we look at the defence system of a brigade, we were able to see that on one of the maps, that area of the brigade would be some 6 kilometres and also in depth, and there it would have its battalions deployed that would cover 3 kilometres in depth, length, et cetera. So that would be the area where the forces are deployed and all these combat activities would be in the area of these brigades, and we could see how many command posts there were at all different levels. We said that there were 14 brigades in that relevant period which means that there would only have been -- there would only -- only the brigades themselves would have 14 command posts and they would not be on the forward line. They would be in the depth. You would have, of course, communication centres, then you would have support units deployed, the police deployed, the Supreme Command of the BH Army. The Presidency became the Supreme Command later. They would also constitute a legitimate target. So of course, there would be in these areas a lot of targets, military targets as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now scroll down the page completely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the movement of troops a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Although it is not your document, paragraph numbered as 2 refers to outgoing mixed rounds or incoming mixed impacts. What does this mixed round or mixed impact mean, if you could tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This sort expression is not used, mixed projectiles. It's not a military term, Your Honour, so it's very difficult for me to tell you what this implies, mixed impacts. Perhaps what they mean is the calibre that were different. It could be from 120 millimetres up to 155 millimetres. That would be the howitzer, et cetera. So perhaps that's what is meant by mixed impacts. I am not aware of any other terms that could have the similar meaning. And if I place myself in his shoes, in his mind, I don't see how else I could interpret the meaning of it because he is referring to artillery. It is possible that you have contact fuse shells. It's possible they would be used for targets that would be live personnel, or piercing shells, but it's not very probable that he was referring to those. He probably meant the different calibre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the end of his answer, General Galic, page 55, lines 1 and 3, clearly repeated the existence of civilian targets in the depth as well, and this precise type of information in the depth is not in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. Civilian targets in the depth?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is definitely a translation issue. General Galic simply said at the very end of his last answer the following thing: There were military targets and not civilian targets, military targets, but he said that these targets were in the depth, and this part, "in the depth," is not mentioned in his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show item 3 a bit further down. This is fine. Item 3, which reads, and I'll read it out in English to have better interpretation: "[In English] Papa 5 OP (Zuc area) and Papa 1 headquarter received impacts within 100 millimetre today. Shrapnel hit Papa 5."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there an indication here that the Serbs opened fire here, and is this different from what you were sent, where you were being told that the Serbs were firing?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this isn't something that we can draw a conclusion. We concluded with the Prosecutor yesterday that we could not establish what the direction from which the shells was fired was and therefore we can't say who is responsible. So we can't tell who fired these shells but it's from the sector of Zuc where Papa 5 was located for a period of time. It was located next to cannons themselves up at Zuc, the Muslim cannons. So they opened fire from these recoilless guns or what else they had up there. They were even assets of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that were captured when Zuc fell. So I recall the assets used very well, and it was from there that they targeted our forces. I do remember clearly that we alerted the observation post to that, and we asked them to relocate their position, to settle further away from these various cannons so that they would not be at risk. So I remember this clearly. But one cannot say who fired at them. Somebody seems to have been persecuting Papa because they didn't want them to be there, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I meant. Mr. President, yes, I did mean Papa 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we just look at the warring party movement here. You mentioned: "[In English] A large number of BH troops were observed moving towards Zuc area, possible rotation." [Interpretation] This movement or this manoeuvre, was that a legitimate target? We're talking about a rotating column, a column in midst of a manoeuvre. Would that be a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, yesterday when I spoke to Madam Prosecutor about plans and other things relating to artillery, one of the elements that was assessed was possible movements of troops and their arrival. So this would be a legitimate military target, like many others. At that particular moment, the moving column was a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go to the following page to look at another paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we leave it. At the top of the page it reads: "Papa 5 observation post and others received impact within 100 metres today," and you answered to the question from Mr. Karadzic that the origin of this fire cannot be concluded with certainty from where it came from. Do you remember having answered so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sure I said that. I said many other things, but I wouldn't go into those details at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But at the same time you also stated that this Papa 5 was located just next to the ABiH cannons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's also true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then do you think it was possible that -- for the units which was located just next to the Papa 5 shell that Papa 5 observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably towards not those units but some other units that wanted to provoke our activity and to create such conditions which would be conducive to a conclusion that the facilities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were being targeted. It would not be the first time that something like that happened. I'm sure that you've had testimonies to that effect here before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this document does not say Papa 5 was hit. It hit 100 -- a location which was 100 metre away from Papa 5. Is it possible, in your opinion, that Bosnian troops shelled their own troops? Do you have that kind of experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have all sorts of experiences from the war in Sarajevo, and I have such experiences as well. I understand your question. I put the same question myself, because that was very close to the deployment of their troops and the distance of 100 metres where those shells fell. I don't know who measured the distance, but it's neither here nor there. If we say that the shells and -- for them the security zone has to be at least 200 metres, this means that they were outside of that security zone, that they were within the danger zone in practical terms. That would be one part of my answer. Secondly, when you have such cases and where nobody actually establishes where the fire came from, then you don't have enough information to establish who was it who opened fire. We can only follow a logic that one would soon be able to conclude that it was the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that opened fire on that area, but we can't be a hundred per cent sure of that. And as soon as you're not certain, it's very difficult to take any measures. That would be my answer, and I don't know whether I have managed to answer your question. I did try, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next page. Bullet point 3 is very similar. It says 150 metres away Papa 5 was hit within the 150 metres. Let's assume that it was the units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that did that. What was their target? Was it UNPROFOR or those cannons, because we saw in the other document that Cutler says, "Even when we moved away, fire continued being opened on that place." What would have been the target of your units if we assume that it was them that opened fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting from all of my orders, instructions, as well as the orders of my commanders and subordinates, it's logical to conclude, as I've already said to the Presiding Judge, that we have enough elements that it was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps units that opened fire at that area. I can't refute that as I sit here after such a long time. However, if it had been the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, you still have to take into account the cannons that were deployed very close to Papa. And I remember that it was said that Papa 5 had to be moved. I don't know whether we're talking about same situation or whether we're talking about another situation. I don't know. In any case, I know that there were problems with that Papa 5. I stated that yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm looking at the format of the document. Does it consist of two separate documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Excellencies, this is just one document, but we're talking about several different paragraphs. "[In English] Once again, Papa 5 received ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure the number is -- numbering is contiguous. Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't know, but I can certainly look into it. I think it's explained in the statement of a witness who's previously testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objection to the admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3524, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The ERN numbers are 31 and 32, two consecutive numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, you were asked on cross-examination how and when you responded. You mentioned that there were mobile mortars as well. Let's look at a Muslim document, 1D21035.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have a citation for that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not able to give you the exact page and line. The fact is, however, that there were many questions about responding with fire, and it was implied that fire was opened on the city and not on military targets and firing positions. We all remember that the General finally protested and stated that they didn't open fire on the city but on the targets from which fire had been opened at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a document issued by the 7th Mountain Brigade. In yesterday's transcript, you will find it on pages 11 and 12. General, sir, let us see how this military security service reports about fire being opened from a mobile mortar, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, I -- I'm -- I have a concern with respect to the lack of foundation to put a document from the opposing factions to the General. I don't think Dr. Karadzic has asked enough foundational questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you were asked and it was suggested to you that you opened fire on parts of the city under Muslim control. You said that you didn't open fire on the city but on legitimate targets. Did you have information to the effect that there were also mobile mortars that provoked you to open fire, and when they were moved, it looked like you had opened fire on the city?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, yesterday I discussed the situation in Dobrinja with the Prosecutor and I did mention those mobile mortars. Therefore, I said it then and it is now confirmed that they did have mobile mortars, and I said even before that that we had problems surrounding the Kosevo Hospital. And you can see it in their report that mobile mortars fired from positions around Kosevo Hospital and Breka settlement. This is just another confirmation that they did have such assets, that they abused hospitals and other such facilities which should have been protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we now look at the third paragraph where it says that after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before doing so, could the General tell us what this document is about first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is about the activity of mortars belonging to the 1st Corps of the BiH Army, i.e., Muslim forces. They send a report to the command of the 1st Corps to the assistant commander for security, i.e., the security organ in a Mountain Brigade who describes the activity of their mortars. He says when they opened fire, on what day, and at what time, and from what areas. That is why I provided a little bit more explanation about the areas from which those mortars opened fire, and I said that they were on vehicles. Those were mobile mortars, and we can see here that they opened fire from the hospital, Kosevo, and from Breka settlement. They could open fire from any other area. They could move rapidly after having opened fire. That would be that. That's why when we speak about protected facilities, I always ask myself how it is protected, to what extent, and this is what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the bottom of the page and it will become clearer what the General is talking about. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see, General, sir, that after a few minutes, three to four shells were fired in response by the aggressor and those shells landed in Kosevo? And in the following passage it says: Firing shells from a motor vehicle is not a rarity 15 days ago in Hane Osman [phoen] Street at Kosevo Brdo, 97 to 99 in the evening hours there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's unbearable for the interpreters. Read, please, slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreter and to the others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it says here that this was not a rarity, and in the last paragraph it says: "I suggest that wide operative measures be taken in order to explain situations when shells were fired from unknown weapons by an unknown perpetrator, i.e., organiser." General, sir, is it also the command of the 7th Mountain Brigade that demands that a stop be put to that because such fire was always returned?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a very clever report, a very intelligent report, and whoever drafted it was very fair because those security organs had to be original, and here we see that that was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a translation. The participants can see it, and this has been zoomed in for the benefit of the General, whose eyesight is not so good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this warning only confirms that those were illegitimate activities because they were bothered by them as well. So when fire was returned, they themselves also spotted a problem, because they opened fire from a civilian zone or a civilian area, from a civilian facility, and then they moved on. And they even say that they didn't know who had sent them and that was the biggest danger. During the war that's the worst situation. When somebody arrived in your zone of responsibility and opened fire and you didn't know who they were. Those people had to be arrested rather than supported in their activities. And whoever drafted this, and that was the assistant commander for security, Tomislav Juric, really drafted this report very well, a very intelligent person, I must say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us who Tomislav Juric was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see it in the lower right-hand side. It says: The assistant commander for security Tomislav Juric. Judging by the name, he was probably Croat, but he could have also been a Serb. Tomislav could be a Serbian or a Croatian name. Well, he was a Croat, in my view, a member of the BiH Army. On their strength in the corps, they had approximately a thousand Serbs and about 2.000 to 2.300 Croats, and about 2.000 women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Brdo brigade was part of the 1st Corps of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that was the 7th Mountain Brigade, the brigade that held Grdonj in the north. It was a Mountain Brigade belonging to the 1st Corps of the BiH Army. You will remember when I explained the positions of those brigades. That was one of the last mountain brigades. There was the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, the 4th, and the 7th brigade. Its name was changed -- or, rather, it was moved from that position and was replaced by the 15th Brigade, and so on and so forth. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3525, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, on page 12 of yesterday's transcript, during the cross-examination you were asked about snipers and protests. What was the goal of your snipers? What were the targets on the other side? What were the targets and why did your snipers exist in the first place?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question was whether the General's evidence was that his sniping activities by his snipers was exclusively military on military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not objecting to the questions themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, why are there snipers, and what are they supposed to achieve on the other side?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained what we imply under snipers and what a sniper is. Other explanations that its any infantry weapon is something I do not accept. The task of the snipers is primarily to return enemy sniper fire, firstly. Secondly, to target some prominent personalities. If it's an officer, then the sniper's task is to neutralise or liquidate this person. Thirdly, neutralise bunkers, the openings on bunkers, where you can see a machine-gun, but you cannot approach it and it's difficult to hit it. The sniper notices that and then tries to neutralise the gunner of a tank or whoever it is. Then it can be also used for other important task. So that would be the briefest explanation of where it is used. We focally used it in our zone because we didn't have many snipers, and I said previously that they are used in pairs, and we have seen that the brigade commander had gathered ten snipers and then he issued them separate orders. So the unit had not yet been formed, but the tasks were issued, and the snipers had the task to fire mainly and mostly against the snipers of the 1st Corps of the BH Army and all other snipers who were on the right bank of the Miljacka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just answer with yes or no. Does that mean that the 1st Corps of the BH Army had snipers who opened fire on our side of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said early on, in the beginning, that according to our information, there were around 500 snipers in the composition of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. I'm not sure whether the number was constant or not. They had some units which, according to our information, were controlled at the brigade level and they also had special units, such as the Seve or the Larks, who fired on our sides and their sides, and so on, in Sarajevo. This is all something that the Chamber is aware of. It's nothing new.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have a look at 1D5566, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, to be very clear and with regard to what Mr. Galic said, if I remember well, he said earlier on that this was not a unit, actually, but it was a group. I'm mentioning this because in his former statements he said that there were no units as such, and here he clearly said that these were no units but groups. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, is a platoon a unit?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, on one occasion I explained what a unit is. A unit begins with a squad, then a platoon, company --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the General please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you spoke too fast. Interpreters were not able to hear you. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very gladly, Mr. President. Units, when we say a unit, what is it? A unit is a squad, which means around ten people. A platoon, the next unit, comprises around 30 men with various weapons, regardless of what sort of formation it is, whether artillery or engineers. The next higher unit is a company which comprises around a hundred men. The next unit is a battalion, between 3 and 500 people. A brigade is 2 to 3.000. It could be more, 4 or 5.000. For example, the Mountain Brigade where I was included 5.800 men. So the range can be quite big. Divisions are from --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you. I'm satisfied with that, and I believe that the Chamber knows this too. Can you please focus on this order from the 1st Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am sorry, and as I said earlier, I recognise it's very difficult to draw the line, but the questions and the area in the cross-examination -- the question was whether or not sniping by his forces was exclusively military on military, and then we went into a discussion on the definition of sniping, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Karadzic asked the witness to tell us the definition of the sniper. He initiated answering that issue, but could you -- continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so. And now we have another document that Dr. Karadzic has brought up on the screen which is a document from the opposing forces that has, in my submission, insufficient foundation on the part of Dr. Karadzic to put to the General now, and I actually think -- although, again, I'm not saying that it's necessarily irrelevant, Your Honours. I think we're getting outside of the area of cross-examination, and perhaps Dr. Karadzic could establish the foundation, to put a document from the other side, from the opposing Bosnian Army forces to the General before he shows him the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But is he not trying to show that the activities on the part of the VRS snipers were military?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour. Perhaps I rose too soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before that the General referred to the goal of snipers, one of their goals was to neutralise the snipers on the other party. Would it not be sufficient foundation?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, could you tell us how this sniping platoon comprising three battalions fits in at the brigade level with the information you had. We see where it was stationed at the Blagoje Parovic school, across the street from Cenex. How does this order fit with what you knew about enemy snipers and was that the target of your snipers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, the sniper platoon does not comprise three battalions. That's a misstatement of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Let me explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- if you read out the first paragraph. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first paragraph says - this is fine - that a sniper platoon be formed from snipers from the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Motorised Battalions, and what follows, from these battalions, they would take these men and set up a platoon, rather than the platoon would be formed on the basis of the three battalions as a whole. The madam is right. You cannot form a platoon from three battalions, but you take out these men from these three battalions and then you establish the platoon. It's a special sniper platoon which was formed, I think, within the 3rd Motorised Brigade. I think it's the 3rd. So that would be my explanation of -- of it up to here, Mr. President. Is there anything I should add?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the time, Mr. Karadzic. Now, how much more would you need? Just for planning purposes. I'm not pressuring you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only seven to ten minutes. If we could do that before the break, I hope I will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can just scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us whether the Blagoje Parovic school, where they were stationed, and Magros, where they went to eat -- and then if we can show what's at the bottom of the page, please. Magros, where they went for meals. Were these legitimate targets?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were legitimate military targets. They were accommodated there. They would be resting there. The unit was deployed, whether it's resting or waiting, these were legitimate military targets, such areas. No doubt about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3526, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you were asked about investigations and whether you requested any investigations to be conducted, and you referred to Article 90 of the annex to the protocol. Was an investigation requested with regard to Markale, a joint investigation, a mixed international investigation, in accordance with that protocol?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gvero said, because he attended talks in connection with this, and he requested that a mixed military commission, which we had at the level of the command of the UNPROFOR in the sector, should be set up and investigate it. They said that the UNPROFOR and the BH Army could not guarantee the work of such a commission that would include Serbs. I don't understand how someone would know that the Serbs would be there together with UNPROFOR. Who was supposed to know in order to be able to guarantee safety? So they simply did not want such a commission to be set up and to work. I also said that on one occasion such a commission did do its work at the airport and established that the BH Army forces were responsible for that incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have a look at -- or, rather, I would draw the participants' attention to D2183 and also P1652 in which requests for investigation are expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was a mixed commission set up that would comprise Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, as I said, such a commission for an incident at the airport was set up and Lieutenant-Colonel Ugresic was a member. And I talked about that so I wouldn't repeat myself. In other cases there were not such commissions for the reason that no security could be guaranteed, but after the 5th of February, 1994, there was a commission which had to establish the violations of truce and occasionally that commission was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And with regard to Markale I?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no. Only the UNPROFOR commission did its work. We received a report about that, and it was only later that General Rose and when you were already there -- that was later, after the incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D5546. 1D5546, page 57 in e-court in the Serbian version, and page 34 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the pages to come up, let me just add that I also ordered, whether on the basis of reports or protests or information I received, that certain investigations be conducted. We could see that yesterday from certain documents. That was my command, to be more precise. It wasn't always me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please focus on Article 90. Was that the article that you had in mind? And Article 89 is the introduction. It says that the in situation of serious violation of conventions and this protocol, the sides will take on themselves the obligation to act joint or separately in co-operation with United Nations. And Article 90 talks about the commission. Can we please see the following page in the Serbian language. And was this the article that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is the article that I am quite familiar with, because on many occasions I referred to it in talks with UNPROFOR representatives. I requested what Madam Prosecutor insisted on: Why did you request to receive a report of a commission? Why would you need that and so on? What was a protest supposed to contain? They here referred to at some point, I'm not sure where, the 4th Geneva Convention and Article 149, which also orders that all serious violations of the conventions be investigated. That was what I referred to, and that's it. 147, Article 147 of the 4th Geneva Convention. It regulates what are serious violations, what is categorised as such. I'm not sure if I have made myself sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please see the lower half of page 2? The page that's on the screen now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please just focus on this, whether you are familiar with it and if that was what you requested. What would be the authorities of the commission?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, under C. Should I read it out? It should "investigate all the facts that are claimed to represent serious violations as defined in the conventions and in this protocol or other serious violations of the conventions or of this protocol." So to investigate all facts. And then the methods and the manner of work of the commission. I wouldn't read it out because I think that everyone is familiar with this and that we would just use up too much time without much benefit, if I were to read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the following page and from item 3 on I will read it. It says five articles -- the bottom, please. Five members of the commission who are not the citizens of any of the warring parties which are appointed by the commission president. And then let us look at the following page. On the basis of the principle of just representation of geographical areas especially taking into account the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there impartiality in the composition of the commissions which investigated this? Was that guaranteed to any of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ho, ho, you see, those commissions that were set up, that were in Sarajevo, they were not fully in accordance with the provisions of Article 90, but I did refer to it, because if we didn't know how to do it, then at least we should do as it is written here. So we would have some sort of legal justification how this should be worked, what sort reports to send, how this is done, what's the method of work, rather than just have the 1st Corps of the BH Army set up some sort of commission and it sends a report and then the UNPROFOR comes to lodge a protest with me, that is to say, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. We did have, or at least I advocated, that the commission should be comprised as appointed, mixed. It didn't have to be completely independent but mixed, with representatives of all three sides, and with this -- this commission should led by UNPROFOR, whether its commander or one of its representatives. And this has to be said. It depends on the level at which the commission would be set up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can several pages be admitted, the ones that we looked at of Article 90 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber does not see the necessity to admit this kind of law. It's part of Geneva Conventions. We have it as a matter of law.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But we can refer to them in our closing arguments; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. One last document. Can we look at D632 briefly. D632.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last remark hopefully. It is important for the General. The General said something which does not appear either in the English transcript or the French transcript. He said: What was necessary in my eyes. And from his point of view, this is extremely important. Page 73, line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last document, D632. General, sir, I asked you earlier what artillery preparation meant and why artillery preparation was done?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I seem to have begun to expound on certain other issues, and I overlooked this. Artillery preparation is done mainly both in offensive and defensive activities. However, it normally precedes an attack. That's when preparations are done in order to neutralise those targets that would place at risk the approach and advance of forces in what is shallow depth as it were. Next, artillery support must be planned and depending on the level of the unit that is being engaged and depending on the stage of the operation that is being addressed, we would have, therefore, as I said, artillery preparation and artillery support.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page. Item 4: I have decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, General, that it said, as it reads here, through a concentration of strong artillery fire in preparation and support fire is to be opened along the route that is planned. And then it further down says: Rout and neutralise the enemy by creating panic among Chetniks and civilians, et cetera. Did this really happen? Did you have experience of this?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, exactly in these areas that are mentioned here, Ilidza, Stupsko Brdo, Zlatiste, in the direction of Dobrinja, Hresa, in the direction of Vogosca and Rajlovac, along those routes they would always be trying to soften the area, as it were, through fire support, fire preparations. They wanted to see if along the fire that they opened, whether they could also deploy infantry and other forces as well. Of course this was the case when circumstances were normal, as it were. However, up at Zlatiste and Hresa, well, for Hresa they would always have preparation. As for Zlatiste, quite a few times they would have no preparation. They would simply climb the hill and suddenly be up at the plateau, and they managed to surprise us this way on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did mention it and the participants can see themselves that in all these items we have artillery support mentioned, and it is stated which unit is to be launched from where. Let me ask you this, General: Did you carry out artillery preparations directed at the town of Sarajevo, and did you ever have a plan, action, or operation aiming to capture an area of the town which would imply artillery fire first and that fire was planned to come from your corps?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, we did have such cases and I did mention them. It was at the time when we were mounting an attack at Otes. We had artillery preparations preceding, certain targets were neutralised. However, this was very difficult in this area because there was reinforced concrete there and we really didn't have the assets that would enable us to do this efficiently. There were artillery preparations for a number of attacks at Zuc and Vraca, the area that we lost, or in the direction of Zabrdje. We had artillery support also when we were taking back recapturing certain areas. We had to have artillery support in those instances as well. As for some other attacks directed at the town that would involve preparations on our part, no, we didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Otes is said to be in the inner core of town. Can you tell the Trial Chamber where this is?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in Ilidza. It's an area of Sarajevo in the direction of Hadzici. It is ahead of Blazuj on the right side. So you would have Ilidza, Blazuj on the right-hand side and then you have a neighbourhood called Otes. And if you recall, I said that across from Otes there was Golo hill and that Otes was only 800 metres away from Golo hill, and there was always a danger for the 1st Corps to link up there. And in that case, the entire area of Ilidza would be completely encircled and cut off and it would have been done for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday at page 11 you were answering the question of why Grkovic was replaced. He didn't have any depth. Can it be seen in this document that Nedzarici was a target of the attack, on page 1, item --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And this document was not properly introduced to the General. This is a document from the ABiH forces, signed by -- and by the way, the translation, the English translation is incomplete, and there's no basis for the General to comment on this document. We don't know if he's seen the document. It's -- the way this has been set up is simply inadequate, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber agrees with Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I may be quite inept since I'm taking -- I'm rushing through it and I'm an amateur. Please consider that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you need time, we can a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do hope that I will finish. This is the last question. What would have happened, General -- or, in other words, did such artillery preparations have to be responded to and what would have become of Nedzarici had this attack of theirs been successful in cutting through to Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we spoke about Grkovic and his battalion yesterday, it was deployed in the area of Nedzarici. We could see that some elements of five brigades were confronting the battalion that was under constant pressure. Can you now picture a commander who has only a small area across -- through Kasindolska Street to pull out in the direction of Ilidza? In this area I think it's Kasindolska Street. If I'm mistaken, I apologise. If that area is cut off and linked up with Sokolovic Kolonija, in that case the unit is left there without a way out. Under such conditions and force with such power that made quite a few crimes in Pofalici and Trnovo, and they knew very well what was coming their way if the BH corps came their way, to be a commander and to have to issue commands constantly for two years under such circumstances, you can imagine his state of mind. I know, I was in Lukavica where shells were landing every day, and believe me when I tell you that this is really taxing on a person. It will exhaust you. You can perhaps live through it for two or three months and after that it becomes unbearable, and that's why the individual had to be removed from the area although he fought there very courageously. And that was my answer in relation to that gentlemen and Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If I were allowed to, I would pay a great deal of compliments to you for your work and conduct but I will only thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I merely wanted to relate a bit of the truth of Sarajevo to all of us to the extent that I know, and, of course, I would very much like all those who know more to come here, it's their duty, because Sarajevo deserves it, from one side and the other. Finally, I would like to -- I don't know if I am allowed to say anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless my colleagues have a question for you that, that concludes your evidence, General Galic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague again to give it, but before -- can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our thanks also goes to you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, for your assistance. The Chamber will take a break and given that the Chamber has an extensive session this time, we will -- the Chamber is minded to have an hour break. So we'll resume at five to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to thank the Chamber as well as all the people who contribute to its functioning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to thank you for the very fair treatment of me from -- that I was afforded by the Tribunal and from both sides who were very fair and correct in their questions to me. The only problem that bothered me was the fact that light was lit during the night and that created quite a few difficulties for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have a safe journey back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Martic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. I just would like to say that I am here as the counsel assisting Mr. Martic, and I would like with the leave of the Trial Chamber to be assisted by an interpreter during his testimony, just in case I have to intervene and speak with Mr. Martic during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Probably Mr. Martic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Martic is well aware of this, but I would rather repeat. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Martic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of Evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this Rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstance would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, President Martic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you give a statement to my Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you, and I recall myself that we make breaks between question and answer and speak slowly so that everything is recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up in e-court 1D07360.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see in front of you the statement that you gave to my Defence team? Is that the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the statement that I gave to your Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for interpretation, and I kindly ask you to do the same. Did you read the statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the last page, please, so that he may authenticate his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom as were put to you when the statement was taken from you, would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement, 92 ter statement, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this statement is being tendered under seal, and a public redacted version is found at 1D07361, which we would also tender as a public exhibit, and the difference is that the last sentence of paragraph 63 has been redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yesterday I remember I said that the Chamber would like to hear from the parties as to the relevance of paragraph 42, 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're prepared to do that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Simply the statements that are the basis of those paragraphs were taken from the admitted exhibit which is the plea agreement of Milan Babic. So in Milan Babic's plea agreement, which the Chamber has admitted as paragraph -- as Exhibit P758, certain assertions were made, and those assertions are rebutted by Mr. Babic in those -- by Mr. Martic in those paragraphs. So we believe that since the exhibit forms a part of the factual information that was presented during the Prosecution's case, that its relevant to and even fair -- only fair that we be given a chance to rebut that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But Mr. Babic's plea agreement was admitted only for the purpose of assessing his credibility, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand it that way, because it seems like we had the practice of admitting exhibits for all purposes. So once something is admitted, even if that may have been the basis for its admission, I don't understand that it can only be used by the Chamber for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would also -- first of all, I should begin by saying we're essentially in agreement with the Defence on the admissibility of those paragraphs. With respect to this particular issue, I think it has been understood -- the plea agreement contains a factual basis, and I think that factual basis has generally been understood when someone testifies to be incorporated into the representations made by that person when he acknowledges and accepts the plea agreement and the accompanying factual basis. So it's an additional reason in support of those advanced by Mr. Robinson, I think. Beyond that, I would also -- sorry, I would also add that we agree that it can only be fair if the Prosecution is permitted to advance these propositions that the other party is entitled to rebut them with such evidence as they have. And even if the material is not independently relevant, this material dealing with the parallel structure and members of the JCE, of course, has independent relevance as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The portions of evidence related the setting up of the parallel structure were excluded from Mr. Babic's transcript. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll -- the Chamber will receive both versions of Mr. Martic's statement. Shall we give the number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 1D7360 will be Exhibit D3527, under seal, and 1D7361 will be Exhibit D3528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, there are a total of 14 associated exhibits being offered with the statement. Six of them are being offered for admission in full, and eight, which are the intercepts, are being offered for being marked for identification at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regard 65 ter number 5280, 5306, 14472, 14481, 14485, I meant five items, these five items, in the Chamber's view do not form an inseparable and indispensable part of the statement in the sense that statement can be understood without these underlying documents. For that reason, the Chamber will not admit those five items. And in the motion, the accused moved to tender 65 ter 5278 as an additional associated exhibit of Milan Babic's 92 quater package, but given that the Prosecution did not seek tender that document and that his testimony could be understood without admitting this document, we will not admit that document, i.e., we'll deny the request. Those intercepts will be admitted being marked for identification. So the numbers for those exhibits will be given in due course by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And we won't tender those documents that you've excluded and we'll simply try -- lead live the document 05278.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just note that there appears to be a difference between the B/C/S version of the statement, which does not have the footnotes, and the English version of the statement, which does have the footnotes. I don't know how that came about because I was involved in the final packaging of these two statements, so what I propose, Mr. President, is that between now and Monday we will prepare another version that will be shown to the Prosecutor in terms -- including in B/C/S which has the footnotes so that the two are identical. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out the summary of President Martic's statement slowly in English. [In English] Milan Martic is former president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, now in Croatia. From late 1990 until 1996, President Martic had many telephone conversations with Radovan Karadzic and attended meetings with him. He believe that they had well over 50 contacts during that period. Most of their discussions before April 1992 involved efforts to avoid the dissolution of Yugoslavia. Dr. Karadzic wanted to preserve Yugoslavia and to use all peaceful and diplomatic means to do so. He was a major factor in convincing the Serbs in Croatia to accept the Vance Plan which brought United Nations troops to Croatia. Mr. Martic found Dr. Karadzic to be an extremely tolerant man with no hatred for Muslims or Croats and with no desire to create a pure Serbian territory. Dr. Karadzic recognised that whatever solution was found for Bosnia and Croatia would involve substantial numbers of one group living as minorities in the territory governed by another group and that their rights would be fully respected. There was never any plan to expel Muslims or Croats from the Bosnian Serb-held areas and certainly no joint criminal enterprise to achieve such a plan. During the war, President Martic attended meetings between Fikret Abdic, a Bosnian Muslim leader from north-western Bosnia, Radovan Karadzic, Slobodan Milosevic, and others. Dr. Karadzic liked Abdic and agreed with his non-fundamentalistic approach for Bosnia. In expressing his support for Mr. Abdic, Dr. Karadzic showed that he had no desire to expel or commit crimes against Muslims. Mr. Martic refutes the evidence of Milan Babic that Slobodan Milosevic and Radovan Karadzic planned to force Slovenia and Croatia to leave Yugoslavia and to have that part of Croatia which was occupied by the JNA remain in Yugoslavia. He states that from his contacts with the two men, there was never any plan or desire that Slovenia or Croatia leave Yugoslavia on the part of Slobodan Milosevic or Radovan Karadzic. Both Slobodan Milosevic and Radovan Karadzic opposed Babic's plan in 1991 for unification of the Krajinas. Serb Krajina in Croatia and Bosnian Krajina. They favoured the preservation of Yugoslavia without changes in the borders. Mr. Martic refutes the evidence of Milan Babic that the Yugoslavia -- Yugoslavian National Army engaged in a war so that the territories it captured would not be left with any Croatian inhabitants. He states that for his contacts with the JNA officers, he never understood that the JNA had a goal of expelling Croats from their homes. Mr. Martic refutes the evidence of Milan Babic that the JNA mistreated Croatian prisoners. He relates one occasion in August 1991, after Croatian policemen were -- had been prisoner in Kijevo where General Mladic took custody of 45 of the prisoners on behalf of the JNA. Upon taking custody of them, he treated them to a dinner at a local restaurant and released them. Mr. Martic refuse -- refutes the evidence of Milan Babic that the attack on Kijevo was the beginning of a plan for the forcible permanent removal of the non-Serb population from Serbian-dominated area of Croatia. Milan Martic states that civilians left Kijevo after he issued a warning that military operation would be commencing there to remove a blockade that had cut off vital supplies to Serbian villages. Mr. Martic refutes the evidence of Milan Babic that Radovan Karadzic used the fact of Martic's arrest on 8th of September, 1991, in the northern Bosnian village of Otoka, as an excuse to stir upset ethnic tensions. To the contrary, Dr. Karadzic urged restraint among Bosnian Serbs while his release was being -- Martic's release was being negotiated. Thanks in part to the intervention of Dr. Karadzic and his strenuous efforts to avoid violence, Mr. Martic was released on the afternoon of 9th of September without any loss of life and a wider war in Bosnia was averted. That would be a short summary, and for that moment I do not have questions for President Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson told us that you would lead live one document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise. I thought that the letter was admitted. However, I would like to ask President Martic. I would like to call up 65 ter 05278.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in your testimony -- or, rather, when Mr. Babic testified in your case, you presented a letter that the late Babic had sent to The Hague Conference on Yugoslavia on the 5th of September, 1991. Do you remember that letter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The letter was written by the late Milan Babic, and he signed it as well. It was adopted by the government on the 5th of September, 1991. I was a member of that government, so I remember the moment when that document was created. We used it here for a very simple reason. What he wrote to the peace conference on Yugoslavia and to the nine other addressees that he sent it to is completely different interpretation of the events that happened during that time as opposed to how he testified here. If we look at that letter and look at it realistically, many of the indictments would not exist. Many of us would not have been on trial here. I hope that this Trial Chamber will take this document into consideration and that it will be able to look at Milan Babic as he was then and as he was when he testified in my case, because we are talking about two completely different persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this letter contain elements which he mentioned later, especially concerning myself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. Here he talks about the struggle for survival. He warns various institutions as to what was going on in Croatia and in the territory of SAO Krajina. He wanted to participate in the international conference in order to be able to explain that. He describes the nature of the new Croatian government. He calls it a neo-fascist government. He compares them to the notorious NDH that was created by Ante Pavelic and supported by Adolf Hitler during the period of 1941 and 1945. He truly testifies in this letter about what was going on. Later on, in his testimony in the Milosevic, Krajisnik, and my cases, the difference was drastic. Finally, when this document was shown to him, he committed suicide, unfortunately. He hanged himself. And the Trial Chamber said that he had died. He -- anybody in the right state of mind can distinguish between a normal death and a suicide. After he was shown this document he committed suicide. I don't know whether he has been ridden with remorse. I was very sorry to hear that, but I knew that he was a sick man. Not only did I know that, everybody else knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you -- when you -- when you say that he was sick, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Whoever spent some time with him could notice that he suffered from some psychological problems, and even as a layperson I could spot his paranoia, his narcissistic nature. As a layperson, I'm not an expert, but I could share with you some details of his health.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you don't need to. I just wanted to -- you to tell us what kind of sickness. Mr. President, as we look at this letter and as -- if we compare it to his testimony about the same events, which of the two testimonies are true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: What he wrote in his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection to this witness offering factual testimony. I do object to purported expert analyses, particularly those that weren't even noticed. So if Mr. Karadzic wants to lead this witness through events about which he has information, which he observed, or received information about, that's one thing, but he's moving down an inappropriate path now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger's observation. If you deal with specific events, that's fine, but in a lump sum way, in this way, it's not appropriate for a witness to comment in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll ask about facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, what was your position in the government of Krajina at the time? Did you attend the session that adopted this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: At that time, in September 1991, I was the minister of the interior in the government headed by Dr. Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this adopted by the government as a reasonable account of the events?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: It was unanimously adopted and it reflected the events with a hundred per cent accuracy. I would not say a word differently to what he wrote at the time and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: I can corroborate this with some facts, some of which relate to my first indictment. The difference in the indictment was caused by the testimony of Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sure that we will have opportunities to do that during cross-examination. You said that there is a significant -- a significant difference between this letter and the late Babic's testimony in the Milosevic, Krajisnik, and Martic cases. How would you describe this difference?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
