utterances.text: The difference is huge. Here he talks about the role of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Objection. I'm sorry, Mr. Martic. Don't --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw and I tender this letter into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3538, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any more questions for the witness, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case in its most part has been admitted in a written form, i.e., through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, although the issue of your indictment and trial was raised to some extent in the recent questioning you had with Mr. Karadzic, there is simply a brief reference to that trial in the statement that you provided the Court and that was admitted earlier today, and that's at paragraph 11, where you note that you were found guilty of committed of crimes committed in Croatia between August 1991 and December 1995. And I wanted to focus a bit more fulsomely on the conviction for your participation in those events. First of all, the crimes that are referred to in paragraph 11 included murder, torture, cruel treatment, imprisonment, deportation and other inhumane acts, persecution, and attacks on civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I noted that although your statement makes reference to events in Kijevo, it did not refer, insofar as I could tell, to some of the events in other locations in Croatia. For example, it did not refer to the events in Hrvatska Dubica where 41 civilians were murdered in October 1991 by the Milicija Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I have an objection to this because his evidence is limited to things that have been admissible in this case. So these things are not in his statement because they're not part of the evidence that's been admitted so far, and its unfair then to imply that somehow this is an omission that these things are not in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Robinson wants to -- is welcome to draw whatever insinuation he thinks may be made by that, but the question is an accurate one. There's a factual representation made in the statement, and I'm asking about the reality of the events that are referred to there, i.e., the crimes for which he was convicted as alluded to in paragraph 11. Now, if Mr. Robinson feels there's an insinuation he doesn't like, that may or may not arise from the juxtaposition of those facts but it doesn't preclude the question being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how is it relevant to this case, Mr. Tieger? Can we not move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President -- okay. I'm willing to move on but let me answer the question. This is a witness who has been brought in here to attest to the benign nature of the people with whom he was in contact, indeed, as you'll hear in a moment, the people with whom he was -- he participated in a joint criminal enterprise for which he was convicted. I think it is instructive for the Court to know the crimes that occurred as a result of that joint criminal enterprise and this witness's participation, particularly when he's trying to convince the Court that he's in a position to persuade you about the benign intentions of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that said, as you said, please move on, Mr. Tieger, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Among the allegations you make in your statement, Mr. Martic, is the one at paragraph 23 where you assert that the -- and as was repeated in the summary by Mr. Karadzic, that the allegation of a joint criminal enterprise in which Radovan Karadzic and yourself were members with the objective to expel Muslims and Croats from the Serb-held areas of Bosnia and Croatia is entirely wrong. The fact is, Mr. Martic, that you were convicted of just such a joint criminal enterprise, that is a joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove the majority of the Croat, Muslim, and non-Serb population from one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia and from large parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: No. I would like to answer your first question, because that bothers me, what the -- what somebody mentioned, the gentleman mentioned. May I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I'm following you. What question do you have in mind, Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where he speaks about crimes in Hrvatska Dubica and with which I was charged and convicted for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, I said that it would not be relevant to this case. Could you please answer the question now asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question was simple, Mr. Martic. You claim in paragraph 23 there was no joint criminal enterprise with Dr. Karadzic to forcibly remove Muslims, Croats, and other non-Serbs from large portions of Bosnia. And the question is: Isn't it true that you -- that in fact you were convicted of participation in a joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove Croats, Muslims, and other non-Serbs from territories in the Republic of Croatia and from large parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: It is true that I was convicted, but I absolutely claim that there was no joint criminal enterprise. This is a construct that was made by this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic -- excuse me, sir. Sorry. Let me just try to identify some ground rules, if I may, because I'm not happy when I have to interrupt a witness and shout over your responses, but I ask you to focus on the question. The particular question was, of course, whether or not it was true that you were convicted. You answered that question and then you began to explain your view on the particular construct that was used and so on. I've been given a certain amount of time to ask you particular questions. I'm trying to frame my questions in a way that allows me to use that time as efficiently as possible, and where the question in fact may call for an explanation, the Court will give you a chance to do that; but where the question is fairly simple, that is, isn't it true that you were convicted of that, and you can answer it as you did, then I ask you to co-operate with the effort to make these proceedings as efficient as possible and simply focus on the question. If you feel unfairly constrained, Mr. Karadzic can both ask for elaboration in redirect and the Court can intervene to allow you to expand on an answer where it's appropriate to do so. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Well, it is okay, but the way I understood your question was that I was supposed to agree with you that there was indeed a joint criminal enterprise. That is one thing. And then you asked me whether I was found guilty and convicted for that charge and I said yes. But we're talking about two totally different issues here, two totally different questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, then you misunderstood the question. The question was whether or not you were convicted for a joint criminal enterprise as I explained it and you answered it in the affirmative. Now, let me answer [sic] a follow-up question to that. It's also true, isn't it, that in that particular case, your case, the Trial Chamber not only found beyond a reasonable doubt that you participated -- there was a joint criminal enterprise and that you participated in it and therefore were responsible for various crimes, but the Court also found that among the -- those others who participated in the joint criminal enterprise were Slobodan Milosevic, Ratko Mladic, and the accused, Radovan Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: That's how it was. That was the Court's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me -- let me call up quickly -- we have limited amount of time today. We will be adjourning in about five minutes. I just want to call up quickly 65 ter 09000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, can you identify, please, the persons depicted in that photograph, and tell us, if you recall, when it was taken.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Personally, of course, I remember these people. They are my friends. I believe that the photo was taken sometime in 1994. Of course I know everybody. Do you want me to name them? But you know them yourself, don't you. You know who these people are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One way or another one of us has to name them, so why don't you go ahead and just name them, moving from left to right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. The first one is Stojan Zupljanin. Sitting next to him is Franko Simatovic, and then Momcilo Krajisnik. Jovica Stanisic is the next one, President Dr. Radovan Karadzic, myself, and the person standing behind me is Dragan Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And although I didn't ask this as part of the earlier question, it's also correct that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic were also found by the Court to be participants in the joint criminal enterprise for which you were convicted by the Trial Chamber in your case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know they have not been convicted yet, and personally I don't think why they should be. There's no reason why they should be convicted of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You may be confusing their case with the findings in your case. I just simply wanted you to confirm as indicated in paragraph 446 of the Trial Chamber judgement in your case that, like Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Mladic, and Mr. Karadzic, Jovica Stanisic and Frenki Simatovic were found to have been participants in the joint criminal enterprise charged and found in your case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC
utterances.text: It's says in their indictment that they were members of that notorious joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance. The interpretation that the gentleman received was that the two of them have already been convicted, which is why he answered the way he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I understood there to be some confusion which is why I re-asked the question as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your statement also states in paragraph 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At this point, given the nature of the answers, I tender the relevant portions of 25046 which is the Trial Chamber judgement. As well as the photograph, which is 09000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're tendering part of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just paragraph 446 at this point. We'll see if we have to amalgamate others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think there's any need to make a judgement into evidence. You can refer to it in -- or the parties can refer to it without being in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine. I have no problem if it's judicially noticed in that manner. So in that case, I just tender 65 ter 09000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, do you know where was it -- where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish you could give me one of those photos to keep as a souvenir. I would love that. This is a celebration, a commemoration of something. I can't remember what. Could you please give me one such photo as a gift, as a souvenir, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can print out if you want, but it is not the time to discuss who should keep the original. But my question was where this photo had been taken, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I can't remember where it was taken. I recognise the people. I believe that we celebrated something, which is why we met, but I don't know exactly where. I believe that the photo was taken in 1994, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If it is convenient, shall we adjourn for the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We might as well at this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we adjourn, I'd like to issue an oral ruling. I think we can do it in the presence of the witness. The Chamber refers to the accused's 79th motion for finding of disclosure violation filed on the 24th of April, 2013, in which he seeks an express finding that the Prosecution violated Rule 66(A)(ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence by failing to disclose three documents, i.e., two information reports and one set of interview notes pertaining to Tarik Kupusovic, Milorad Bircakovic and Vahid Karavelic, by the 7th of May, 2009, deadline for the disclosure of such material. The accused also seeks a remedy for the repeated violation by the Prosecution of its disclosure obligations and repeats his request that the Prosecution be ordered to make its database available to his Defence team. The Prosecution responded on the 8th of May, 2013, and argued that the motion should be dismissed given that the accused "fails to claim or show that he was prejudiced by the late disclosure" of the material in question. The Prosecution acknowledges that the material should have been disclosed under Rule 66(A)(ii) by the 7th of May, 2009, dead-line. The Prosecution emphasises that the accused made no attempt to identify or substantiate any prejudice caused by the late disclosure and this could warrant summary dismissal of the motion. The Prosecution further observes that Kupusovic was reclassified as a reserve witness in July 2010 and was never called to testify. Similarly, Karavelic was dropped as a Prosecution witness in December 2010, and Bircakovic's evidence was admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Prosecution further contends that there was no prejudice given that the newly disclosed material "adds nothing new of any substance to the information already possessed by the accused," and in any event, it would be open for the accused to seek to add Kupusovic and Karavelic to his witness list if he wanted to elicit the information contained in the new material or seek reconsideration of the Rule 92 bis decision not to call Bircakovic for cross-examination. The Chamber having reviewed the newly disclosed material finds that the Prosecution violated 66(A)(ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence with respect to these three witnesses. However, considering that Kupusovic and Karavelic did not ultimately testify in this case and the third witness, Bircakovic, was a Rule 92 bis witness, and in the absence of any attempt by the accused to assert any prejudice with respect to the late disclosure, the Chamber finds that the accused was not prejudiced by these disclosure violations and in the absence of prejudice dismisses the remainder of the motion. The Chamber reminds the accused of its instruction in the decision of the accused's 77th and 78th disclosure violation motions that: "The accused should not consider the process of filing disclosure violation motions to be a numerical exercise of recording each and every violation. The accused should instead focus on how a specific violation has caused him prejudice and how any newly disclosed material could have within used by him to advance his case in light of the material already in his possession. It is one thing to argue that multiple documents have been disclosed in violation of the Rules, but such violations are unlikely to cause prejudice if the contents of the newly disclosed material adds nothing new or of any significance to material already in the accused's possession." On my part, I refer to my partially dissenting opinion in the Chamber's decision on the accused's 37th to 42nd disclosure violation motions and decline to make a finding of violation in the absence of prejudice to the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If I may without contesting ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll entertain your views later on. Mr. Martic, Mr. Martic, we are going to adjourn for the week, and we will resume on Monday at 9.00 in Courtroom III instead of Courtroom I only for that day, and I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. I take it you understood that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of May, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
